newsitem.title: CANADA: TENNIS-WOODRUFF AND KUERTEN REACH CANADIAN OPEN FINAL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-WOODRUFF AND KUERTEN REACH CANADIAN OPEN FINAL.

text.p: Unseeded American Chris Woodruff's dream run reached the final of the Canadian Open after he knocked out his fourth seeded player of the week with a semifinal victory over Russian Yevgeny Kafelnikov Saturday.
The 57th-ranked former U.S. collegiate champion put himself in position to claim his first career title with a hard-fought 5-7 7-5 6-3 victory over fourth-seed Yevgeny Kafelnikov.

"It's great to be a giant-killer, especially if the game is close and the crowd gets behind you," said Woodruff, who also ousted 16th seed Jan Siemerink, second seed Goran Ivanisevic and seventh seed Mark Philippoussis en route to the final, where he will face French Open champion Gustavo Kuerten of Brazil.
In the day's other upset, the sixth-seeded Kuerten thoroughly outplayed top seed Michael Chang for a lopsided 6-3 6-1 victory.
"He was hitting pretty clean off the ground and serving quite well," Chang said. "I really didn't have a chance to get into the match."

The victory over Chang guaranteed the 20-year-old from the seaside city of Florianopolis a spot in the top 10 in the next ATP Tour rankings, making him the first Brazilian to reach such lofty heights.
"It would be great even if 20 or 30 other Brazilians had been in the top 10," Kuerten said. "After all the work I did, after all the travelling, I'm getting my bonus, my payback."
Woodruff's run looked like it might come to an end more than once Saturday.
He blew his chance to take the first set when his serve deserted him with a 5-3 lead. Unable to close out the set, Woodruff allowed Kafelnikov to win four successive games to claim the opener.
Both players held serve until the 11th game of the tight second set when Woodruff finally converted his fifth break point of the game with a spectacular backhand volley winner.
After managing to force a third set, Woodruff raised his level of play, especially on the critical points.

He scored the lone break of the set for a 4-2 lead and emphatically solidified the advantage by belting four consecutive aces to reach 5-2 -- with a little help from basketball superstar Michael Jordan.
"It's weird the way my mind works out there," admitted the Tennessee native, who also closed out the match with an ace.

"I hit the first ace and I started thinking about Michael Jordan. When the game is on the line, Jordan takes over. When I break serve in a big match like this, I think about how someone like Jordan would take over the game. So I step up to the line and try to give myself positive thoughts like that."
Whatever the strategy, it worked.
"It was my best performance of the tournament and I didn't win the match," Kafelnikov said. "He definitely deserved to win. He played better than I did."
And Kuerten played way better than world number two Chang, the highest-ranked player the Brazilian had ever beaten.
Following a short rain delay with the score at 2-2 in the first set, Kuerten went on a rampage of spectacular shotmaking that overwhelmed Chang.
He rocketed ground strokes from the baseline that had the 25-year-old veteran scrambling in vain to reach them.
Kuerten also made 69 percent of his first serves and won 79 percent of the points when the first serve was good.
"When a player is in that kind of groove, you've got to attack him a little bit and give him a smaller target to hit to. I just wasn't able to do that enough," Chang said.
The pro-Kuerten crowd seemed amazed by the potency and dominance of the colourful Brazilian.
"I hope I can play like that everyday," Kuerten said, "but I think it's more just one night when you can be like that."
